text_map.central_idea: Speaking from centuries after her death, the speaker remembers dying as a polite, unhurried carriage ride with a courteous Death. The ride passes images of a whole life and stops at a grave described as a sunken house. Only at the end does she reveal that she slowly realized the ride led to eternity. The calm, mannerly surface keeps death's finality half-hidden until the last stanza.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: A first-person speaker who has died. She looks back from an eternity that has lasted 'centuries' to the day Death called for her. She was Death's passenger and, in effect, the woman he was courting.

devices.function: Turns Death into a polite gentleman caller, so a feared event looks like a social courtesy.
The vocabulary of manners and courtship gives the encounter a decorous, almost romantic feel.
The repeated 'We passed' strings together stages of life (childhood, ripeness, decline) as scenery going by.
The setting sun stands for the end of life and the coming of death.
The grain seems to watch the speaker go by, as if the living world is looking on while she leaves it.
Presents the grave as a house, a new home, without ever naming it.
Calmly describes the sunken tomb in architectural terms, softening the horror of burial.
Centuries feel shorter than one day, which shows how much the moment of realization weighed on her.
The calm ride ends with the speaker finally understanding that its destination was eternity.

items.stem: The personification of Death in ([[r1]]) primarily serves to

options.text: present death as a courteous caller, making a feared event seem a polite visit
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Kindly' and the act of stopping for someone make Death a considerate gentleman, so dying looks like a social courtesy.
options.evidence_quote: He kindly stopped for me

options.text: portray death as a menacing pursuer who seizes the speaker against her will
options.label: reversal
options.why: Death stops 'kindly' and acts with 'civility'. Nothing about him is threatening.
options.evidence_quote: For his civility

options.text: suggest that all people secretly long for death as a welcome release from their toil
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The poem tells one speaker's experience. It makes no general claim about what all people long for.

options.text: show that the speaker literally refused to halt her carriage for a stranger
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: 'Could not stop' is figurative: she was too busy living. She did not literally refuse anything, and she did not own a carriage.
options.evidence_quote: Because I could not stop for Death

evidence_quotes: He kindly stopped for me

items.stem: The description of who rides in the carriage ([[r1]]) suggests that the relationship between the speaker and Death is best characterized as

options.text: intimate yet formally chaperoned, like a decorous courtship
options.label: correct
options.why: The two ride alone together ('just ourselves'), but Immortality rides along like a chaperone, and the stress on 'civility' keeps things formal.
options.evidence_quote: The carriage held but just ourselves

options.text: openly hostile, a tense contest between captor and captive
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Death behaves 'kindly' and the ride is leisurely. There is no hostility.
options.evidence_quote: He kindly stopped for me

options.text: secretly romantic, a reunion of two long-separated lovers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the poem says the two had met before. 'Reunion' and 'long-separated' have no basis in the text.

options.text: intimate but crowded, since many other passengers ride along
options.label: partially_right
options.why: 'Intimate' fits, but the carriage holds only the two of them and Immortality, so it is not crowded.
options.evidence_quote: And Immortality

refs.quote: The carriage held but just ourselves

evidence_quotes: The carriage held but just ourselves

items.stem: Taken together, the speaker's statement that she "could not stop for Death" ([[r1]]) and her admission that she "had put away" her pursuits ([[r2]]) suggest that she

options.text: was too absorbed in living to seek death, yet yields to it entirely and willingly
options.label: correct
options.why: At first she is too busy to stop. Then she sets aside both labor and leisure 'For his civility', a complete and gracious surrender that sits uneasily with how busy she was.
options.evidence_quote: My labor, and my leisure too

options.text: resists Death's summons throughout and is carried off only by superior force
options.label: reversal
options.why: She puts her life aside out of courtesy. There is no resistance and no force.
options.evidence_quote: For his civility

options.text: regrets chiefly the loss of her work, which she abandons with deep, bitter reluctance
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: She gives up 'leisure too', not just work, and the tone is calm rather than bitter.
options.evidence_quote: We slowly drove, he knew no haste

options.text: had long planned for death and so had already ended both work and pleasure
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Reads 'had put away' as advance planning. The opening line shows she was not ready or waiting for death.
options.evidence_quote: Because I could not stop for Death

items.stem: The sequence of images in the third stanza, moving from the school ([[r1]]) to the grain ([[r2]]) to the sun ([[r3]]), primarily serves to

options.text: trace the stages of a life, from childhood through maturity to its close
options.label: correct
options.why: Children at school stand for youth, ripe grain for maturity, and the setting sun for the end of life. The order follows the course of a lifetime.
options.evidence_quote: We passed the school where children played

options.text: map the actual route of the carriage through the streets of the speaker's village
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: No road leads past the setting sun. The images are symbolic, not a literal route.
options.evidence_quote: We passed the setting sun

options.text: show the speaker growing more fearful as the journey nears its end
options.label: reversal
options.why: The pace stays leisurely and the speaker never shows fear.
options.evidence_quote: We slowly drove, he knew no haste

options.text: contrast the busy labor of the living with the idleness of the dead
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The children are playing, not working, and the images are arranged as a progression, not as a contrast between labor and idleness.
options.evidence_quote: Their lessons scarcely done

items.stem: The speaker's description of the house in the fourth stanza ([[r1]]) affects the reader's interpretation chiefly by

options.text: inviting the reader to recognize a grave the speaker never names directly
options.label: correct
options.why: A 'house' that is 'A swelling of the ground', with a roof barely visible and a cornice that is only a mound, is clearly a grave. The speaker keeps calling it a house, so the reader has to supply what she leaves unsaid.
options.evidence_quote: A swelling of the ground

options.text: establishing that the journey ends at the speaker's new home among the living
options.label: literal_for_figurative
options.why: Takes 'house' literally. A dwelling that is only a mound in the ground is a grave, not a home among the living.
options.evidence_quote: The cornice but a mound

options.text: revealing that the speaker deliberately lies to conceal her terror of burial
options.label: unsupported
options.why: 'Seemed' marks an honest impression, not a lie, and the speaker never shows terror.
options.evidence_quote: a house that seemed

options.text: suggesting that the speaker's entire account of the journey is only a dream
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Treats one veiled image as if it cast doubt on the whole poem. The speaker says centuries have really passed since that day.
options.evidence_quote: Since then 't is centuries; but each

items.stem: The final stanza functions primarily to

options.text: shift to a vantage beyond death, revealing where the ride was always headed
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Since then 't is centuries' moves the speaker into eternity, and the stanza reveals that the horses were headed 'toward eternity' all along.
options.evidence_quote: Since then 't is centuries; but each

options.text: return the speaker to life, ending the journey before it reaches its goal
options.label: reversal
options.why: The stanza confirms that the ride's destination was eternity. It does not bring her back to life.
options.evidence_quote: Were toward eternity

options.text: express the speaker's anguish at the endless, weary boredom of her centuries dead
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: She says the centuries feel short, not weary, and she shows no anguish.
options.evidence_quote: Feels shorter than the day

options.text: describe the horses in detail, adding a last image of the carriage itself
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The horses' heads matter for the direction they point, which is what she realizes. They are not there as description.
options.evidence_quote: I first surmised the horses' heads

items.stem: In context, the word "surmised" ([[r1]]) most strongly suggests that the speaker

options.text: grasped the journey's destination only gradually, by inference
options.label: correct
options.why: To 'surmise' is to guess from clues. Together with 'first', it shows a slow, tentative dawning of what the ride meant.
options.evidence_quote: I first surmised the horses' heads

options.text: knew from the very first moment exactly where Death was taking her
options.label: reversal
options.why: 'Surmised' describes a guess, not certain knowledge from the start.
options.evidence_quote: Feels shorter than the day

options.text: was surprised and alarmed when she noticed where the horses were facing
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Confuses 'surmised' with 'surprised'. The ride is calm and shows no alarm.
options.evidence_quote: We slowly drove, he knew no haste

options.text: doubted that the carriage was moving toward any destination at all
options.label: unsupported
options.why: What she surmised was a definite destination: eternity.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the speaker's situation as the poem presents it?

options.text: She speaks from beyond death, recalling the day Death came for her
options.label: correct
options.why: She says centuries have passed since the day of the ride, so she is speaking from eternity and looking back on her death.
options.evidence_quote: Since then 't is centuries; but each

options.text: She is a dying woman imagining the funeral that awaits her tomorrow
options.label: reversal
options.why: The ride is told in the past tense as something that already happened. She is not looking ahead to it.

options.text: She is a mourner describing a friend's carriage ride to the grave
options.label: misread_speaker
options.why: Death stops 'for me'. The speaker herself is the passenger, not an onlooker.
options.evidence_quote: He kindly stopped for me

options.text: She speaks moments after death, still riding toward the graveyard
options.label: partially_right
options.why: She is dead, but she speaks centuries after the ride, not while it is happening.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is the most defensible thesis about the poem as a whole?

options.text: Through Death's courtly manners and the unhurried ride, the poem turns dying into a calm passage whose finality emerges only gradually
options.label: correct
options.why: Death's 'civility' and the slow pace make dying gentle. The disguised grave and the late 'surmised ... eternity' show that its finality dawns only slowly. The claim is specific and covers the whole poem.
options.evidence_quote: I first surmised the horses' heads

options.text: The poem argues that all human fear of death is irrational, since every life, however busy, ends in the same peaceful eternity
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The poem presents one speaker's experience. It makes no argument about everyone's fears.

options.text: Through images of decay and darkness, the poem depicts death as a cruel abductor who violently tears the speaker away from a life she cherishes
options.label: reversal
options.why: Death is 'kind' and civil, and the speaker gives up her pursuits willingly. Nothing is violent.
options.evidence_quote: He kindly stopped for me

options.text: The third stanza's catalog of school, grain, and sunset is the poem's central achievement, a pastoral portrait of village life
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Focuses on one stanza and misses its symbolism. The setting sun points to death, not to village life.
options.evidence_quote: We passed the setting sun

text_map.central_idea: The speaker recalls a calm, courteous carriage ride with Death. It passes the stages of life and ends at the grave. From the vantage of 'centuries' later, she shows that death has changed her sense of time, making eternity feel briefer than the single day she understood where she was going.
text_map.speaker_or_narrator: A first-person speaker, apparently already dead, looking back on the day Death called for her and the journey that followed.

items.stem: A student claims that the poem shows death changing the speaker's sense of time, so that vast spans come to feel brief. Which of the following quotations provides the strongest evidence for this claim?

options.text: "Since then 't is centuries; but each / Feels shorter than the day"
options.label: correct
options.why: Here the speaker says that centuries feel shorter than a single day. This states directly that, after death, vast spans of time feel brief.
options.evidence_quote: Since then 't is centuries; but each

options.text: "We slowly drove, he knew no haste, / And I had put away / My labor"
options.label: partially_right
options.why: These lines describe the slow pace of the ride itself. They do not show long periods of time feeling short afterward.
options.evidence_quote: We slowly drove, he knew no haste,

options.text: "We passed the school where children played, / Their lessons scarcely done"
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: This image shows a stage of life the speaker passes. It is about what she leaves behind, not about how she now perceives time.
options.evidence_quote: We passed the school where children played,

options.text: "We paused before a house that seemed / A swelling of the ground"
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: These lines identify where the journey ends, at the grave. They say nothing about how long spans of time feel to the speaker.
